title: Replacing deliver.rdr with op:listen?
body:
I'm going to open some issues for things that have been discussed on IRC/matrix.

Full transcript for this one below, but I will try to summarize: Goblins has an extra `listen` message type that doesn't exist in E's CapTP or Cap'n Proto. As I understand it this message tells the receiver that it should send the actual data associated with a promise. I suggested that this message could actually just entirely replace the `rdr` field in `deliver` or `Call.sendResultsTo` in capnp, and provide a bit more flexibility.

Something not mentioned in the discussion, but, I think with this in place doing "fire and forget" messaging becomes fairly simple:
just send the `deliver` and immediately follow it with a `gc-answer` (with the caveat that capnproto's version of `gc-answer`, `Finish`, is allowed to cancel side effects, so we might want to fuss with that).

```
@zenhack:matrix.org : I don't see a listen op here: http://erights.org/elib/distrib/captp/index.html and I don't think any of capnp's messages are equivalent either; what exactly is op:listen?
cwebber : isd: you're right, and this is a consequence of taking a Lambda The Ultimate approach to this. Subscribing to a promise doesn't necessarily mean a miranda method. there was a reason this came up in the design, and I need to get it written down. Zarutian_HTC did a translation in his port to and from what Agoric expects
however I can't talk about this at the second
I will document it and put it on the tracker soon though
@zenhack:matrix.org : Cool, I look forward to reading about it.
@zenhack:matrix.org : Hazarding a guess: is it just an explicit operator for "please send me the result," in contrast to capnp's Call.sendResultsTo field? I can see how splitting that off into a separate message would allow a bit more flexibility; right now I think at least both go-capnp and haskell-capnp just always set sendResultsTo = caller, since the API makes it hard to know in advance when the results won't be needed.
cwebber : isd: yes, it's separate
yeah you got it
@zenhack:matrix.org : cool.
cwebber : oh
also
@zenhack:matrix.org : Yeah, and I can see why doing lambdas by default would make that particularly necessary.
cwebber : isd: messages sent with <- do have a "reply-to" field
however
it's for non-question promises
or rather non "return-style"
it's also because of promise pipelining
being able to send an arbitrary message to any object
er
to any promise, before its result appears
well, if you are doing it lambda-centric rather than method-centric
then you need to be able to distinguish between "I'm sending this because I want to subscribe" and "I'm sending this because I want to invoke it"
or even invoke what it eventually pints to
point
s
because some actors might even capture all message arguments
eg proxies of various kinds as appear in dynamic ocap patterns
@zenhack:matrix.org : Yeah, I'd surmised.
@zenhack:matrix.org : Is reply-to part of the protocol, or do you just feed it in as an extra argument to call with the result?
Zarutian_HTC : cwebber: hmm?
cwebber : isd: it's part of the protocol, there's a DeliverOp and DeliverOnlyOp, like in E
@zenhack:matrix.org : Are we just talking about the rdr argument for DeliverOp?
(I grepped for reply-to and didn't find it in captp.rkt, so I assume it's called something else in the code)
(In this case I assume resolve-me-desc)
I guess if you want to defer the decision, you could just give it some null value and then separately op:listen. But I now doubt I understand what op:listen actually does.
...since I would expect it to obviate that argument.
cwebber : isd: ah yeah I guess it's resolve-me
not reply-to
isd: sometimes you want to listen to a promise when you aren't just invoking an actor
(on <some-promise> (lambda _ ...))
that's different than
(<- <some-promise> ...)
or even (define some-promise (<- <some-actor> ...))
but all that might be eliminated
isd: right now we don't auto-setup a full proxy for a foreign promise, it's only eg when the equivalent of E's when happens. that maybe should/will change.
Zarutian_HTC : cwebber: not nescisarily that it has to change
if that promise is just being passed around and eventual-sent-to then the vat that got given the promise might not even care about what it resolved to
Zarutian_HTC : regarding rdr in deliverOp in both spritely goblins and E is that it could be: a) redirector for resolving the promise made by that eventual-send, b) could be such redirector but from a diffrent vat (could be handedoff or non-transparently proxied), c) such a redirector for a promise on the vat that recieved this deliverOp, or d) a local ignorer or just null for the cases when we want to promise pipeline but do not care about the interme
sorry, should be: do not care about the eventual results of such intermediary promises
re NonceLocator in CapTP of E: we know it handles turning SwissNums from sturdyrefs targetting this vat into live refs. It also handles the handoff stuff via .acceptFrom() and .provideFor() methods.
I have in my notes somewhere additions I wanted to make to the NonceLocator
one is handling invocation certificates (see capcert on erights.org iirc)
Zarutian_HTC : that one can have a tree of possibilities tbd: should these certs be ActiveCerts (look for ActiveCerts by Nikita iirc in comp sci papers) and so on. But they badically boil down to similiar functionality as sturdyrefs though they offer a bit more, like offline unforeseen attenuation of authority, spellserver like functionality (see Brian Warners blog, can dig up link on request) and so on
another addition to NonceLocator in similar vein but not authority bearing is a seqBlock constructor 
seqBlocks need a bit of explanation: they are basically like an CapTP connection session excerpt but with 'holes' like quasiLiterals have
a seqBlock is basically like a Smalltalk80/Squeak or Ruby block: it can take arguments and has a list of eventual sends to do. Basically like straight line code.
the aforesaid seqBlock constructor gets as its arguments, a seqBlock description (basically arrays being (ab)used as Scheme like lists for structure), initial environment (a map from names to objects), and an allowence bundle to pay for its gas and rent
but this stuff is way up the protocol support levels like described in capnproto's rpc.capn
btw, what that seqBlock constructor returns is basically an lambda/function/closure
and such could be passed in as the rdr of an deliverOp or the callback/errback of an op:listen message
"oy! when x resolves, do these things for me, ok?" kind of functionality
@zenhack:matrix.org : So, from a design perspective, is there a reason to actually keep rdr/resolve-me if we have listen? It seems like it becomes unnecessary. For simply returning to the caller, you can op:listen immediately after op:deliver. For cases where you would pass it a resolver that lives in the receiving vat, you just make the call yourself and pass it the answer as a promise. For an object on a third vat, you could do the provide/accept dance to pass the result to that vat instead.
Zarutian_HTC : hmm... that is actually quite a good idea
it would make the d) option in my enumeration above implict
it would also make the code use support on sending side for d) pretty much fall out for free iff op:listen is only done due to (on ...) / .then() / E.when()
this in turn makes the bandwidth, serialization/packing and such costs go down
though we need to figgure out how to tease the 'decider/resolver' authority out of rdr for those cases where the deliverOp reciving vat wants to pass that to a diffrent vat.
basically the first aforesaid vat can go 'oy, you handle this for me and let the customer know about the results' to the vat it is 'subcontracting' to
'let the customer know about the results' is the aforementioned authority needed to be teased out of rdr
@zenhack:matrix.org : Couldn't they just return the promise they get from the "subcontractor?" Which would go through the usual handoff logic if it's a third party vat.
Zarutian_HTC : hmm... the promise and its resolver live on the vat that sent the original deliverOp
an example to illustrate: Alice lives on VatA and has a live ref to Bob who lives on VatB
that live ref is over an connection between VatA and VatB
in the code of Alice there is js`const bar = Bob~.foo();`
the captp machinery in VatA gets that invocation via BobProxy which is the local standin Alice has direct access to (BobProxy is one of the half circle things in the granovetter diagrams in CapTP of E literature)
that machinery makes a promise resolver pair for the eventual results of this invocation
the machinery says on the connection to VatB: okay, a dilverOp for you, I am using wireid x to name the eventual result of this invocation for promise pipelining purposes, here is the resolver/rdr for that promise, this wireid Bob is the target of this invocation, the verb is 'foo' and here are the arguments
@zenhack:matrix.org : I guess my thinking would be, instead, the machinery would arrange such that (assuming js notation) the first call to .then (if any) triggered the listen message.
Zarutian_HTC : the captp machinery on VatB's end of the connection gets that, deserializes the arguments and sticks the eventual send in its event loop queue
part of the eventual send thing in the queue is the resolver/rdr which gets invoked sendOnly style with the result when VatB gets around to process that eventual send
so VatA effectively handed VatB the head of the eventual ref-arrow of the ~.foo() result promise
op:listen afaict is for when the tail of such eventual ref-arrow is being handed around and the party it got handed to is interested to learn of what it eventually points to
isd: the above is how this works in CapTP of E and possibly Agoric also. 
erights is this correct re Agoric?
we could have it so that the promise, and its resolver, for the eventual result lives instead on VatB in the above example 
which means if Bob subcontracted the ~.foo() stuff to Carol on VatC then VatB would use aforesaid resolver to 'resolve' to promise living on VatC. That would cause the handoff you mentioned, isd
@zenhack:matrix.org : Yeah, that's more or less what I had in mind.
Zarutian_HTC : the .then() machinery in the ocapn for op:listen provoked deliverOnlyOps would need to beware of such promise substitution
s.
this change might well be worth it to get the aforesaid bandwidth, serialization/packing costs gains
@zenhack:matrix.org : Making it easy to not transmit results in the middle of a pipeline seems useful.
Zarutian_HTC : though we might want to expose 'create a local promise, give its resolver to this oneArgFunc, and return the promise' desc:«tbd» might be something we might want to have
* Zarutian_HTC sees how 'mighty' that last post was, unintentionally
but that is for less common mostly esoteric looking stuff
```
